issues.legal_issue: An erroneous property number in a sale decree and certificate does not defeat the sale when the property’s identity is otherwise clearly established.
material_facts: The final decree and sale certificate stated plot number 160, while the property intended was plot 1060.
The khata number, area, and boundaries in those documents corresponded to plot 1060, and there was no plot 160 in that khata.
The writ for delivery of possession and the later sale deed correctly identified plot 1060.
issues.conclusion: The number was a mere misdescription, not an uncertainty about the property’s identity, so the appellants’ challenge to the respondents’ claim to the plot failed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Thakur Barhma v. Jibon Marware and Gossain Das Kundu v. Mrithujoy Agran Sarda, a fully identified property may be treated as sold despite a misdescription that does not create doubt about its identity. Rambhadra Naidu v. Kadiruja Sami Naicker was distinguished because it involved a dispute about the identity of the property, rather than a mere error in its description.

predicates.appeal_against_possession_decree: A party appealed from a decree granting possession of property.
predicates.sale_documents_contain_property_number_e: The decree or sale certificate contained an incorrect property number.
predicates.other_description_details_match_one_prop: The other identifying details in the sale documents corresponded to a particular property.
predicates.no_property_has_the_stated_number_in_the: No property with the number stated in the documents existed in the relevant record.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges possession based on a sale and the documents contain a wrong number but their other details identify one property and no property bears the stated number, the property’s identity remains established despite the misdescription.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot claim subrogation on behalf of mortgagees who redeemed an earlier mortgage when the later mortgage contains no agreement for subrogation.
material_facts: The property had been subject to an earlier mortgage, which was later redeemed by payment to the earlier mortgagees.
The appellants sought to rely on subrogation in favour of the later mortgagees, on whose behalf they claimed to hold the property.
The later mortgage deed did not mention the earlier mortgage and did not show that money had been retained to redeem it.
issues.conclusion: In the absence of an agreement for subrogation, the appellants could not establish a subrogation claim on behalf of the later mortgagees.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the later mortgagees could be subrogated to the earlier mortgagees’ rights only if there was an agreement that they would be so subrogated. An agreement might have been inferred had money been left with them to redeem the earlier mortgage, but the mortgage deed did not support that inference. No statute or earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_against_possession_decree: A party appealed from a decree granting possession of property.
predicates.appellants_assert_subrogation_for_later_: The appellants sought to rely on subrogation on behalf of later mortgagees.
predicates.earlier_mortgage_was_redeemed: Payment was made to discharge an earlier mortgage.
predicates.no_subrogation_agreement_shown: The later mortgage deed and other evidence did not establish an agreement for subrogation.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a possession decree involves a claim of subrogation on behalf of later mortgagees who redeemed an earlier mortgage, the claim is not established if no agreement for subrogation is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A possession defense based on holding property on behalf of mortgagees fails when the record does not establish that their mortgage remained in force or that the appellants held the property on their behalf.
material_facts: The appellants contended that they were entitled to remain in possession through later mortgagees whose mortgage had not been affected by an earlier mortgage suit.
There was no evidence establishing that the later mortgage remained in force when the earlier suit was brought or that the appellants held the property on behalf of those mortgagees.
The High Court found that the evidence showed the appellants were in possession at least by a later time.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not resist the respondents’ claim for possession on the basis that they held the property on behalf of the later mortgagees.
issues.legal_principle: A party relying on a mortgagee’s continuing rights to resist possession must establish that the mortgage remained in force at the relevant time and that the party held possession on the mortgagee’s behalf. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this ruling.

rule.if: appeal_against_possession_decree and defense_relies_on_possession_for_mortgagees and mortgage_continuation_at_suit_unproved and possession_for_mortgagees_unproved

predicates.possession_for_mortgagees_unproved: The record did not establish that the appellants held the property on behalf of the mortgagees.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a possession decree involves a defense based on possession for mortgagees, the defense fails if neither the mortgage’s continuation at the relevant time nor possession on the mortgagees’ behalf is established.
